Your first game, one step at a time

A practical guide to
Aesir Gameworks.

Set up your studio. Shape an idea. Build, test, and release your game with a clear next step.

Beginner friendly73 workflows140 skillsFully self-contained

Start here

Aesir Gameworks gives Hermes Agent a set of game-development instructions: workflows for common jobs, specialist roles, reusable templates, and quality rules. You describe the game and make the important decisions; Hermes uses these instructions to help you plan, build, review, and test it.

Keep two folders separate. The Aesir repository contains the studio profile. Your game has its own workspace, containing its code, designs, and plans. Run game workflows in the game workspace.

You do not need to learn every skill. Start with /studio-start, follow one next step at a time, and use /studio-help whenever you are unsure.

Kind of skill What it means for you
Workflow A repeatable job you start with a slash command, such as /brainstorm.
Role A specialist perspective Hermes can delegate to, such as game-designer. These are instructions for AI agents, not human staff.
Rule Practices that apply to particular game files, such as UI or gameplay code.
Core/support Routing, workspace setup, templates, engine references, memory policy, and framework quality checks.

How to use this file: read the getting-started sections first. Use the skill search when you need a particular job. Expand a skill for its complete instructions and bundled references. The guide, styles, search, and SVG diagrams are all inside this file; no internet connection is needed to read it. External attribution links are optional.

Install and open your game

1. Check the prerequisites

Install and configure Hermes Agent with a working model/provider, and have Git available. This distribution requires Hermes 0.21.0 or newer. Install the engine you intend to use when you are ready to build or test the game. An engine-reference skill does not install the engine itself.

Bash runs the profile hooks. jq and Python 3 enable additional hook validation. On Windows, make Git Bash available on your PATH.

Run these in your terminal, not as chat messages:

hermes --version
git --version
bash --version
jq --version
python3 --version

2. Install the profile

Replace /path/to/aesir-gameworks with the folder containing this distribution:

hermes profile install /path/to/aesir-gameworks --name gameworks --force --yes
hermes profile info gameworks
hermes profile use gameworks

profile use sets the default profile for later Hermes sessions. Installation updates the distribution-owned files. Credentials, memories, sessions, and unrelated skills are preserved. Leave off --force-config unless you deliberately want to reset the profile’s local configuration.

3. Open a separate game folder

For a new game, for example:

mkdir -p ~/Projects/my-first-game
cd ~/Projects/my-first-game
hermes

For an existing game, change to its existing project folder instead. If Hermes asks you to trust the profile hooks, review the hook descriptions in this guide before accepting.

4. Start the conversation

Type this inside Hermes chat:

/studio-start

Tell it whether you have no idea yet, an idea, existing designs, or an existing game. Give your engine/version if known, target platform, available time, experience, and a small first goal. “I am new to game development. I want a small single-player game and can spend four hours a week” is enough to begin.

/gameworks loads the studio routing guidance. /project-bootstrap creates the workspace context and technical-preferences template when needed; /setup-engine fills in the engine, version, conventions, and budgets. Existing files should be preserved.

5. Check that setup worked

You should have a game-local AGENTS.md and docs/technical-preferences.md. After /setup-engine, these should name your engine and version rather than placeholders. Run /studio-help for the next useful action.

Update later

hermes profile info gameworks
hermes profile update gameworks --yes

Use update when the recorded source is the intended distribution. If the profile has no source, repeat the install command with the correct source. Updates preserve local config.yaml; /skin gameworks changes the theme from chat without resetting that configuration.

Talk to your studio

A slash command starts a workflow. Text after the command gives its subject, mode, or file. Run the examples one at a time, read the result, and answer any questions before moving on.

/brainstorm a small exploration game
/design-system movement
/design-review design/gdd/movement.md

Replace example names and paths with your real ones. A path like production/epics/<epic>/<story>.md is a placeholder, not a file that already exists. Each skill’s expanded instructions explain its arguments and prerequisites.

What to provide

  • Goal: what you want the player or developer to be able to do.
  • Context: relevant files, engine/version, platform, and existing decisions.
  • Boundaries: what is included, what is excluded, and your time budget.
  • Success: what you should be able to observe or test when it is finished.

For unresolved design decisions, expect a question, a few options, a decision, a draft, and approval before writing. An explicit request already authorizes its stated edits; it should not need approval again for every file. A larger scope or new material decision may need your input.

A workflow ending with “done” means that workflow finished. Read its output and follow-ups; it does not automatically mean the feature is tested, the stage is passed, or the game is released.

Choose a review mode

Mode What runs When to use it
lean (default) Director reviews at phase gates; intermediate director gates are skipped. A practical starting point for a solo developer or small team.
full All applicable director gates. When you want frequent feedback and can spend more time/model usage on reviews.
solo No director gates. /gate-check still checks artifacts. Short experiments where you accept less expert review.

The workspace stores this in production/review-mode.txt. Gate-using workflows accept a per-run override, such as /design-system movement --review full. These modes control director reviews, not your creative decisions or proof that tests passed. Labels such as Heavy/Medium/Light in skill details describe intended model tiers; they do not wire particular models automatically.

From idea to release

Follow this route for a new project. For existing work, use the adoption recipe below and fill the gaps rather than starting over.

Stage Do this Result to look for
1 · Concept /brainstorm, /setup-engine, /design-review, /art-bible, /map-systems. Try /prototype if the core idea is risky. A game concept, clear pillars, visual direction, engine pin, and a systems map.
2 · Systems Design /design-system for each minimum viable system; /design-review each; then /review-all-gdds and optionally /consistency-check. Approved system designs with rules, formulas, edge cases, and acceptance criteria.
3 · Technical Setup /create-architecture, /architecture-decision for key decisions, /architecture-review, /create-control-manifest; initialize tests with /test-setup; begin /ux-design. Architecture, accepted Foundation decisions, requirements traceability, engine references, tests/CI, accessibility requirements, and interaction patterns.
4 · Pre-Production Prefer /vertical-slice and /playtest-report before detailed planning. Complete /asset-spec, key-screen /ux-design and /ux-review; then /create-epics, /create-stories, /sprint-plan new. Validated core loop, complete art direction, reviewed menu/HUD/pause specs, and ready work for the first sprint.
5 · Production Plan QA, check story readiness, implement, review, test, and close stories. Run /team-qa sprint after the sprint’s stories. Working features with acceptance evidence and an updated sprint tracker.
6 · Polish /team-polish, /perf-profile, /balance-check, /asset-audit, bug fixes, and /playtest-report. Better performance, usability, balance, and documented player feedback.
7 · Release Explicitly request /release-checklist, /launch-checklist, and /team-release; prepare /changelog and /patch-notes. Reviewed release readiness and a coordinated game release. Actual build/deployment results must be verified.

At each transition, run /gate-check. With no argument it proposes the current-to-next transition for you to confirm. The named transitions are:

Command Transition checked
/gate-check concept Concept → Systems Design
/gate-check systems-design Systems Design → Technical Setup
/gate-check technical-setup Technical Setup → Pre-Production
/gate-check pre-production Pre-Production → Production
/gate-check production Production → Polish
/gate-check polish Polish → Release

PASS means the checks are met. CONCERNS identifies risks to resolve or explicitly accept. FAIL identifies missing requirements or blockers. Fix the named gaps and rerun the check. The workflow treats its verdict as advisory to the user; do not confuse choosing to proceed with obtaining a PASS. Stage updates belong in production/stage.txt and must be authorized.

Source differences to know: the overview catalog labels test setup optional in Pre-Production, but the detailed Technical Setup gate requires a working test scaffold and CI, so this guide places it earlier. The Pre-Production checklist calls a vertical slice recommended/non-blocking, while its quality section also asks for a complete, fun-validated slice. Build and playtest one for the least ambiguous path, or explicitly resolve and record the skipped evidence with /gate-check. Review mode also affects whether art/director sign-offs run; a skipped sign-off is not an approval.

Everyday workflow recipes

“I already have a game”

Run /studio-start, /project-stage-detect, then /adopt. Adoption audits format and gaps, producing an ordered migration plan; it should preserve existing work. Target a smaller area with /adopt gdds, /adopt adrs, /adopt stories, or /adopt infra. For undocumented code, use /reverse-document with its real path. Fill design gaps with /design-system retrofit design/gdd/movement.md or architecture gaps with /architecture-decision retrofit docs/architecture/adr-001.md. Review the result before the relevant gate.

“I want to implement my first story”

Start with a real story generated by /create-stories. Its requirement ID, governing architecture decision, dependencies, and acceptance criteria must be clear. Then:

/qa-plan sprint
/story-readiness production/epics/<epic>/<story>.md
/dev-story production/epics/<epic>/<story>.md
/code-review <changed-files>
/story-done production/epics/<epic>/<story>.md

Run the project’s actual tests between implementation and completion review. /dev-story needs docs/architecture/tr-registry.yaml and the story’s governing ADR; missing either blocks implementation. /architecture-review can bootstrap the registry. A missing control manifest produces a warning; generate it from Accepted ADRs. Resolve incomplete story dependencies and stale manifest references before proceeding.

“I am starting another sprint”

Use /retrospective for the last sprint, /sprint-plan new for the next, /scope-check to keep it realistic, and /qa-plan sprint before implementation. Repeat the story loop. Use /sprint-status for progress, /bug-report for discoveries, /bug-triage for priority, and /team-qa sprint to close the QA cycle. /milestone-review checks the larger delivery goal.

“I need to change a feature”

For a small, bounded design change, use /quick-design. For a substantial system, use /design-system. Review it with /design-review; when an existing design changes, run /propagate-design-change to identify affected ADRs and stories. Use /consistency-check for shared entities and /estimate plus /scope-check for schedule impact. Update the affected decisions/stories before implementation.

“I need art, menus, or a complete feature team”

Establish /art-bible first. Run /asset-spec without arguments to build a visual entity/screen inventory, then specify individual assets. It creates specifications and generation prompts; these are not finished art files. Use /ux-design and /ux-review for player flows, screens, HUD, and accessibility. Pick a team workflow when several disciplines need to work together:

Team command Coordinated work
/team-combat Combat design, implementation, and QA.
/team-narrative Story structure, lore, characters, and writing.
/team-ui UX specifications through UI implementation and polish.
/team-level Layout, encounters, environment, and level validation.
/team-audio Audio direction, sound needs, and integration.
/team-polish Performance, visual, audio, and experience polish.
/team-qa Test strategy, execution, coverage, and sign-off.
/team-release Release candidate preparation through deployment coordination.
/team-live-ops Seasons, events, and post-launch content planning.

These workflows coordinate role skills. You supply scope and decisions; the coordinator handles handoffs and surfaces blockers. Tool access, engine availability, and real test evidence still determine what can be completed.

“I found a bug or the game is slow”

Use /bug-report with reproduction steps, expected/actual behavior, and build/platform. /bug-triage prioritizes the backlog. Use /perf-profile for measured performance problems, /test-flakiness for inconsistent CI tests, /regression-suite to prevent recurring bugs, and /tech-debt for longer-term cleanup. A test protocol from /soak-test still needs an actual extended run.

“I want to ship and support my game”

Complete the Polish gate, confirm localization with /localize, then explicitly request release checks and /team-release. Internal /changelog records engineering changes; /patch-notes explains changes to players. /day-one-patch handles known launch issues in a focused patch; explicitly request /hotfix for urgent production incidents. /team-live-ops plans continuing updates. These are game workflows; releasing the Aesir profile itself uses the repository’s contributor release process.

“I want to improve Aesir itself”

Work in the distribution repository, read CONTRIBUTING.md, and use /skill-test to validate workflow/role instructions. /skill-improve runs a diagnose–fix–retest loop; framework-qa supplies quality policy and test specifications. Keep distribution changes separate from game artifacts. Behavior, skill, hook, or packaging changes need an Unreleased changelog entry; only a release request bumps the distribution version.

Testing, files, and continuity

A plan describes a test. A test file implements a test. A passing run is evidence that it passed. A playtest report records what a person actually observed. Keep these separate when judging completion.

Story type Evidence expected by /dev-story
Logic Automated unit test at the story’s test-evidence path.
Integration Integration test or documented playtest record.
Visual/Feel Manual evidence document, typically production/qa/evidence/<slug>-evidence.md. Human playtesting judges feel.
UI Manual walkthrough document or interaction test.
Config/Data Smoke check for the changed data.

Use /test-evidence-review to judge whether evidence is adequate, incomplete, or missing. /story-done checks acceptance criteria and deviations; /smoke-check covers critical paths, /regression-suite checks continuing coverage, and /team-qa coordinates the broader cycle. Missing tools or an unavailable engine should be reported as unverified work, never as a pass.

Find your files

All paths below are inside your game workspace:

Path What it stores
AGENTS.md Project context, engine pin, and workspace instructions.
docs/technical-preferences.md Engine/language, conventions, and performance budgets.
design/gdd/ Game concept, systems map, and system design documents.
design/art/, design/assets/, design/ux/ Art direction, asset specifications, and interface/experience designs.
docs/architecture/ Master architecture, ADRs, requirement registry, traceability, and control manifest.
docs/engine-reference/ Version-specific engine references for the game.
production/epics/ Epics and their implementable story files.
production/sprints/, production/sprint-status.yaml Sprint plans and machine-readable story status.
production/stage.txt, production/review-mode.txt Current stage and review intensity.
production/qa/ QA plans, playtest reports, and manual evidence.
src/, assets/, tests/ Game code, game assets, and tests.
prototypes/ Isolated experimental builds and reports.

Continue after an interruption

Ask Hermes to read the current story, sprint tracker, and any existing authorized checkpoint before continuing. production/session-state/active.md is used only when that checkpoint path is authorized; do not create it for a read-only task or make a competing progress tracker. Session/subagent logs live under production/session-logs/.

Project stage and sprint state belong in the game, not profile memory. USER.md holds stable user facts, MEMORY.md holds compact cross-project environment facts, and reusable procedures belong in skills.

Troubleshooting and glossary

Problem Next step
Slash skill is unavailable Check hermes profile info gameworks, select hermes profile use gameworks, start Hermes from the game folder, and load /gameworks. Confirm the profile installation contains the skills.
“Where do I start?” /studio-start for first use; /studio-help for the next action in an existing session.
Stage seems wrong /project-stage-detect diagnoses artifacts. /gate-check evaluates an actual transition; do not assume a folder’s existence proves readiness.
Design skill cannot find a system Run /map-systems, then supply the real system name to /design-system.
Implementation stops for missing registry/ADR Run /architecture-review for the registry; create or correct the governing /architecture-decision.
Existing documents use another format Use /adopt and retrofit modes to fill gaps instead of replacing them.
Two specialists disagree Creative issues go to creative-director, technical issues to technical-director, and scope/scheduling issues to producer.
Review reports CONCERNS or FAIL Read the specific findings, resolve or explicitly accept risks, then rerun the relevant review. A skipped review is not a pass.
Hooks appear inactive Check hook trust/configuration and availability of Bash, jq, and Python. Missing optional tools can cause checks to skip.
Commit validation blocks a change Fix invalid asset JSON or unowned TODO/FIXME comments in source; inspect the actual hook output.
Theme did not change on update Local config is preserved. Use /skin gameworks in chat.
Skill asks for bundled references Hermes should use skill_view('gameworks', file_path='references/quick-start.md'), for example. A skill name plus a space is not a filesystem path.

Plain-language glossary

Term Meaning
GDD Game Design Document: what the game/system does and why.
Pillar A principle used to decide what belongs in your game.
Core loop The sequence of actions and rewards the player repeats.
MVP Minimum viable product: the smallest coherent game scope.
ADR Architecture Decision Record: a technical choice, its reasons, and constraints.
TR-ID A requirement identifier connecting design, architecture, implementation, and tests.
Control manifest A compact coding-rules sheet generated from accepted architecture decisions.
Epic / story / sprint A larger work package / a small implementable task / a short planned work period.
Acceptance criteria Observable conditions that define when a task is done.
Prototype / vertical slice A quick experiment / a production-quality pass through the complete core loop.
QA / CI Quality assurance / automated integration checks, such as tests on code changes.
UX / HUD Player experience and interaction / the information displayed during gameplay.
Regression / flaky test / soak test A returning bug / an inconsistently passing test / an extended-duration test.
Brownfield / retrofit An existing project / filling gaps in its current documents.
MDA Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics: rules, the behavior they produce, and the player’s experience.

All skills, in one place

Search by name or purpose, then expand a card. Workflow cards contain the exact procedure, including arguments, required inputs, outputs, and recovery steps. Role cards contain responsibilities and boundaries. These advanced instructions are written for Hermes; you can normally let the workflow follow them.

Getting started

/studio-startStart guided Aesir studio onboarding.

Start in Hermes chat with /studio-start and the subject or arguments described below. If a required input is missing, provide it before dependent work continues.

Source: skills/workflows/studio-start/SKILL.md

Guided Onboarding

Model tier: Medium

This skill writes one file: production/review-mode.txt (review mode config set in Phase 3b).

This skill is the entry point for new users. It does NOT assume you have a game idea, an engine preference, or any prior experience. It asks first, then routes you to the right workflow.

Phase 1: Detect Project State

Before asking anything, silently gather context so you can tailor your guidance. Do NOT show these results unprompted — they inform your recommendations, not the conversation opener.

Check: - Engine configured? Read the game-workspace file docs/technical-preferences.md (not the profile template skills/studio/gameworks/references/technical-preferences.md). If the file is missing, or the Engine field contains [TO BE CONFIGURED], the engine is unset. - Game concept exists? Check for design/gdd/game-concept.md. - Source code exists? Use search_files with file_glob under src/ (*.gd, *.cs, *.cpp, *.h, *.rs, *.py, *.js, *.ts). - Prototypes exist? Check for subdirectories in prototypes/. - Design docs exist? Count markdown files in design/gdd/. - Production artifacts? Check for files in production/sprints/ or production/milestones/.

Store these findings internally to validate the user's self-assessment and tailor recommendations.

Phase 2: Ask Where the User Is

This is the first thing the user sees. Use clarify with these exact options so the user can click rather than type:

  • Prompt: "Welcome to Aesir Gameworks! Before I suggest anything, I'd like to understand where you're starting from. Where are you at with your game idea right now?"
  • Options:
  • A) No idea yet — I don't have a game concept at all. I want to explore and figure out what to make.
  • B) Vague idea — I have a rough theme, feeling, or genre in mind (e.g., "something with space" or "a cozy farming game") but nothing concrete.
  • C) Clear concept — I know the core idea — genre, basic mechanics, maybe a pitch sentence — but haven't formalized it into documents yet.
  • D) Existing work — I already have design docs, prototypes, code, or significant planning done. I want to organize or continue the work.

Wait for the user's selection. Do not proceed until they respond.

Phase 3: Route Based on Answer

If A: No idea yet

The user needs creative exploration before anything else.

  1. Acknowledge that starting from zero is completely fine
  2. Briefly explain what /brainstorm does (guided ideation using professional frameworks — MDA, player psychology, verb-first design). Mention that it has two modes: /brainstorm open for fully open exploration, or /brainstorm [hint] if they have even a vague theme (e.g., "space", "cozy", "horror").
  3. Recommend running /brainstorm open as the next step, but invite them to use a hint if something comes to mind
  4. Show the recommended path: Concept phase: - /brainstorm open — discover your game concept - /setup-engine — configure the engine (brainstorm will recommend one) - /prototype — throwaway concept build: validate the core idea is fun before designing (1–3 days) - /art-bible — define visual identity (uses the Visual Identity Anchor brainstorm produces) - /map-systems — decompose the concept into systems - /design-system — author a GDD for each MVP system - /review-all-gdds — cross-system consistency check - /gate-check — validate readiness before architecture work Architecture phase: - /create-architecture — produce the master architecture blueprint and Required ADR list - /architecture-decision (×N) — record key technical decisions, following the Required ADR list - /create-control-manifest — compile decisions into an actionable rules sheet - /architecture-review — validate architecture coverage Pre-Production phase: - /ux-design — author UX specs for key screens (main menu, HUD, core interactions) - /vertical-slice — production-quality end-to-end build to validate the full game loop - /playtest-report (×1+) — document each vertical slice playtest session - /create-epics — map systems to epics - /create-stories — break epics into implementable stories - /sprint-plan — plan the first sprint Production phase: → pick up stories with /dev-story

If B: Vague idea

  1. Ask them to share their vague idea — even a few words is enough
  2. Validate the idea as a starting point (don't judge or redirect)
  3. Recommend running /brainstorm [their hint] to develop it
  4. Show the recommended path: Concept phase: - /brainstorm [hint] — develop the idea into a full concept - /setup-engine — configure the engine - /prototype — throwaway concept build: validate the core idea is fun before designing (1–3 days) - /art-bible — define visual identity (uses the Visual Identity Anchor brainstorm produces) - /map-systems — decompose the concept into systems - /design-system — author a GDD for each MVP system - /review-all-gdds — cross-system consistency check - /gate-check — validate readiness before architecture work Architecture phase: - /create-architecture — produce the master architecture blueprint and Required ADR list - /architecture-decision (×N) — record key technical decisions, following the Required ADR list - /create-control-manifest — compile decisions into an actionable rules sheet - /architecture-review — validate architecture coverage Pre-Production phase: - /ux-design — author UX specs for key screens (main menu, HUD, core interactions) - /vertical-slice — production-quality end-to-end build to validate the full game loop - /playtest-report (×1+) — document each vertical slice playtest session - /create-epics — map systems to epics - /create-stories — break epics into implementable stories - /sprint-plan — plan the first sprint Production phase: → pick up stories with /dev-story

If C: Clear concept

  1. Ask them to describe their concept in one sentence — genre and core mechanic. Use plain text, not clarify (it's an open response).
  2. Acknowledge the concept, then use clarify to offer two paths: - Prompt: "How would you like to proceed?" - Options:
    • Formalize it first — Run /brainstorm [concept] to structure it into a proper game concept document
    • Jump straight in — Go to /setup-engine now and write the GDD manually afterward
  3. Show the recommended path: Concept phase: - /brainstorm or /setup-engine — (their pick from step 2) - /prototype — throwaway concept build: validate the core idea is fun before designing (1–3 days) - /art-bible — define visual identity (after brainstorm if run, or after concept doc exists) - /design-review — validate the concept doc - /map-systems — decompose the concept into individual systems - /design-system — author a GDD for each MVP system - /review-all-gdds — cross-system consistency check - /gate-check — validate readiness before architecture work Architecture phase: - /create-architecture — produce the master architecture blueprint and Required ADR list - /architecture-decision (×N) — record key technical decisions, following the Required ADR list - /create-control-manifest — compile decisions into an actionable rules sheet - /architecture-review — validate architecture coverage Pre-Production phase: - /ux-design — author UX specs for key screens (main menu, HUD, core interactions) - /vertical-slice — production-quality end-to-end build to validate the full game loop - /playtest-report (×1+) — document each vertical slice playtest session - /create-epics — map systems to epics - /create-stories — break epics into implementable stories - /sprint-plan — plan the first sprint Production phase: → pick up stories with /dev-story

If D: Existing work

  1. Share what you found in Phase 1: - "I can see you have [X source files / Y design docs / Z prototypes]..." - "Your engine is [configured as X / not yet configured]..."

  2. Sub-case D1 — Early stage (engine not configured or only a game concept exists): - Recommend /setup-engine first if engine not configured - Then /project-stage-detect for a gap inventory

Sub-case D2 — GDDs, ADRs, or stories already exist: - Explain: "Having files isn't the same as the template's skills being able to use them. GDDs might be missing required sections. /adopt checks this specifically." - Recommend: 1. /project-stage-detect — understand what phase and what's missing entirely 2. /adopt — audit whether existing artifacts are in the right internal format

  1. Show the recommended path for D2: - /project-stage-detect — phase detection + existence gaps - /adopt — format compliance audit + migration plan - /setup-engine — if engine not configured - /design-system retrofit [path] — fill missing GDD sections - /architecture-decision retrofit [path] — add missing ADR sections - /architecture-review — bootstrap the TR requirement registry - /gate-check — validate readiness for next phase

Phase 3c: Write Initial Stage File

After confirming the starting path (and before asking about review mode), write the initial stage to production/stage.txt. Create the production/ directory if it does not exist.

Stage mapping: - Path A, B, or C (starting from scratch): write Concept - Path D, existing project, engine not configured or only a game concept exists: write Concept - Path D, existing project with GDDs but no architecture documents: write Systems Design - Path D, existing project with full architecture (ADRs, architecture doc): write Technical Setup

Do this silently — no "May I write?" needed for this single-line file.

Say: "I've set production/stage.txt to [stage] — this anchors your status line and stage detection."

Phase 3b: Set Review Mode

Check if production/review-mode.txt already exists.

If it exists: Read it and show the current mode — "Review mode is set to [current]." — then proceed to Phase 4. Do not ask again.

If it does not exist: Use clarify:

  • Prompt: "One setup choice: how much design review would you want as you work through the workflow?"
  • Options:
  • Full — Director specialists review at each key workflow step. Best for teams, learning the workflow, or when you want thorough feedback on every decision.
  • Lean (recommended) — Directors only at phase gate transitions (/gate-check). Skips per-skill reviews. Balanced approach for solo devs and small teams.
  • Solo — No director reviews at all. Maximum speed. Best for game jams, prototypes, or if the reviews feel like overhead.

Write the choice to production/review-mode.txt immediately after the user selects — no separate "May I write?" needed, as the write is a direct consequence of the selection: - Full → write full - Lean (recommended) → write lean - Solo → write solo

Create the production/ directory if it does not exist.

Phase 4: Confirm Before Proceeding

After presenting the recommended path, use clarify to ask the user which step they'd like to take first. Never auto-run the next skill.

  • Prompt: "Would you like to start with [recommended first step]?"
  • Options:
  • Yes, let's start with [recommended first step]
  • I'd like to do something else first

Phase 5: Hand Off

When the user confirms their next step, respond with a single short line: "Type [skill command] to begin." Nothing else. Do not re-explain the skill or add encouragement. The /studio-start skill's job is done.

Verdict: COMPLETE — user oriented and handed off to next step.

Edge Cases

  • User picks D but project is empty: Gently redirect — "It looks like the project is a fresh template with no artifacts yet. Would Path A or B be a better fit?"
  • User picks A but project has code: Mention what you found — "I noticed there's already code in src/. Did you mean to pick D (existing work)?"
  • User is returning (engine configured, concept exists): Skip onboarding entirely — "It looks like you're already set up! Your engine is [X] and you have a game concept at design/gdd/game-concept.md. Review mode: [read from production/review-mode.txt, or 'lean (default)' if missing]. Want to pick up where you left off? Try /sprint-plan or just tell me what you'd like to work on."
  • User doesn't fit any option: Let them describe their situation in their own words and adapt.

Collaborative Protocol

  1. Ask first — never assume the user's state or intent
  2. Present options — give clear paths, not mandates
  3. User decides — they pick the direction
  4. No auto-execution — recommend the next skill, don't run it without asking
  5. Adapt — if the user's situation doesn't fit a template, listen and adjust

/studio-helpChoose the next game development step.

Start in Hermes chat with /studio-help and the subject or arguments described below. If a required input is missing, provide it before dependent work continues.

Source: skills/workflows/studio-help/SKILL.md

Studio Help — What Do I Do Next?

Model tier: Light

Read-only. Lightweight orientation, not a full audit. For a gap analysis, /project-stage-detect. Structural keyword COMPLETE is internal — do not print it. The printed done line is studio-help done.

Step 1: Read the Catalog

Read skill_view('gameworks', file_path='references/workflow-catalog.yaml'). That list is authoritative for phases, step order, required vs optional, and artifact globs.

Do not glob (game-workspace)/skills/*/SKILL.md. Do not collect uncataloged skills. There is no "Also installed" footer.

Step 2: Determine Current Phase

Check in this order:

  1. Read production/stage.txt — if it has content, that is the phase. Map it: - "Concept" → concept - "Systems Design" → systems-design - "Technical Setup" → technical-setup - "Pre-Production" → pre-production - "Production" → production - "Polish" → polish - "Release" → release

  2. If stage.txt is missing, infer from artifacts (most-advanced match wins): - src/ has 10+ source files → production - production/epics/ has files (EPIC.md or story-*.md) → pre-production - docs/architecture/adr-*.md exists → technical-setup - design/gdd/systems-index.md exists → systems-design - design/gdd/game-concept.md exists → concept - Nothing → concept (fresh project)

Step 3: Read Session Context

Read production/session-state/active.md if it exists. Extract the current artifact, in-progress task, and STATUS block. Use this for the Focus row and to name the Next target. Do not quote it as a paragraph.

Step 4: Check Step Completion for the Current Phase

For each step in the current phase (from the catalog):

Artifact-based checks

If the step has artifact.glob: - Use search_files with file_glob set to the catalog glob (game-workspace relative) - If min_count is specified, verify at least that many files match - If artifact.pattern is specified, search that pattern on the matched file - Complete = artifact condition is met - Incomplete = artifact is missing or pattern not found

If the step has artifact.note (no glob): read the file the note names when it is a path. Count statuses. Do not mark MANUAL if that file yields counts.

If the step has no artifact field: infer from the same counts when a later/earlier step in this phase already produced them (e.g. Designed vs Approved GDDs). Otherwise mark UNKNOWN.

Mark MANUAL only when there is no file or count to read.

Production: sprint-status.yaml

When the phase is production and production/sprint-status.yaml exists, read it before globbing stories.

  • in-progress → active work (Focus / Next target)
  • ready-for-dev → Next if nothing is in-progress
  • done → complete
  • blocked → include the blocker field in the fact line

Skip glob checks for implement and story-done when the YAML exists.

Repeatable required steps

Counts go on the fact line. Next is this step only while it still has a named item to create. Items that exist and wait on a later required step (review, approve) do not keep this step as Next.

Systems Design: read design/gdd/systems-index.md and the GDD files. Missing GDD → Next: /design-system [system]. GDD exists but not Approved → Next: /design-review [path]. All MVP Approved → advance to /review-all-gdds.

Step 5: Pick Next and Optional

From the completion data:

  1. Next — the first incomplete required step. Exactly one.
  2. Optional — at most one incomplete optional catalog step that can run now and does not replace Next.

If catalog text says the optional runs after a still-incomplete required step, omit it — unless session state queued it now; then keep it and append (does not replace /command).

If the user named a just-finished step (e.g. "just finished design-review"), advance past that step when the artifact check is ambiguous.

clarify only when Next would be MANUAL and there is no count or file evidence. Do not clarify after the report.

If the user passed a topic (/studio-help testing): facts stay. Next is the topic skill only when it can run now; otherwise Next stays the required step and the topic skill may appear as Optional under the same Optional rules. Do not list multiple topic skills.

Do not print upcoming required steps. /gate-check appears only when it is Next.

Step 6: Present Output

Print only this shape. No headings, no Done list, no Coming up, no gate warning, no "fresh session", no skill catalog.

Phase  [Phase Label]
[Noun] [counts or named status — 1–2 lines, current phase only]
Focus  [path] — [short status]

Next: /command  [named target]

Optional: /command (does not replace /next-command)

studio-help done.

Rows

  • Phase always.
  • 1–2 fact lines after it: counts or named artifacts for this phase only (GDDs 8 written · 1 approved (Economy) · 7 Designed, Sprint 4 · 3 in-progress · 1 blocked, Concept missing). Never a completed-step list.
  • Focus only when active.md or an in-progress artifact exists. Omit the row otherwise.
  • Next: exactly one row, always prefixed Next:. If the catalog step has command:, print Next: /command [named target]. If it has no command (e.g. accessibility-doc), print Next: [imperative] [named path] — still that one row, never a paragraph or a second recommendation.
  • Optional: at most one line. Omit the row when nothing qualifies.
  • Done line last, exactly: studio-help done. Print nothing after it.

Never auto-run the next skill.

If nothing exists to infer (no stage.txt, no concept, no engine pin): Phase Concept, fact Concept missing, Next: /studio-start. Do not print a full workflow map.

/project-stage-detectDetect project stage and artifact gaps.

Start in Hermes chat with /project-stage-detect and the subject or arguments described below. If a required input is missing, provide it before dependent work continues.

Source: skills/workflows/project-stage-detect/SKILL.md

Project Stage Detection

Model tier: Light

This skill scans your project to determine its current development stage, completeness of artifacts, and gaps that need attention. It's especially useful when: - Starting with an existing project - Onboarding to a codebase - Checking what's missing before a milestone - Understanding "where are we?"

Workflow

1. Scan Key Directories

Analyze project structure and content:

Design Documentation (design/): - Count GDD files in design/gdd/*.md - Check for game-concept.md, game-pillars.md, systems-index.md - If systems-index.md exists, count total systems vs. designed systems - Analyze completeness (Overview, Detailed Design, Edge Cases, etc.) - Count narrative docs in design/narrative/ - Count level designs in design/levels/

Source Code (src/): - Count source files (language-agnostic) - Identify major systems (directories with 5+ files) - Check for core/, gameplay/, ai/, networking/, ui/ directories - Estimate lines of code (rough scale)

Production Artifacts (production/): - Check for active sprint plans - Look for milestone definitions - Find roadmap documents

Prototypes (prototypes/): - Count prototype directories - Check for READMEs (documented vs undocumented) - Assess if prototypes are archived or active

Architecture Docs (docs/architecture/): - Count ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) - Check for overview/index documents

Tests (tests/): - Count test files - Estimate test coverage (rough heuristic)

2. Classify Project Stage

Based on scanned artifacts, determine stage. Check production/stage.txt first — if it exists, use its value (explicit override from /gate-check). Otherwise, auto-detect using these heuristics (check from most-advanced backward):

Stage Indicators
Concept No game concept doc, brainstorming phase
Systems Design Game concept exists, systems index missing or incomplete
Technical Setup Systems index exists, engine not configured
Pre-Production Engine configured, src/ has <10 source files
Production src/ has 10+ source files, active development
Polish Explicit only (set by /gate-check Production → Polish gate)
Release Explicit only (set by /gate-check Polish → Release gate)

3. Collaborative Gap Identification

DO NOT just list missing files. Instead, ask clarifying questions:

  • "I see combat code (src/gameplay/combat/) but no design/gdd/combat-system.md. Was this prototyped first, or should we reverse-document?"
  • "You have 15 ADRs but no architecture overview. Should I create one to help new contributors?"
  • "No sprint plans in production/. Are you tracking work elsewhere (Jira, Trello, etc.)?"
  • "I found a game concept but no systems index. Have you decomposed the concept into individual systems yet, or should we run /map-systems?"
  • "Prototypes directory has 3 projects with no READMEs. Were these experiments, or do they need documentation?"

4. Generate Stage Report

Use template: skill_view('project-templates', file_path='templates/project-stage-report.md')

Report structure:

# Project Stage Analysis

**Date**: [date]
**Stage**: [Concept/Systems Design/Technical Setup/Pre-Production/Production/Polish/Release]
**Stage Confidence**: [PASS — clearly detected / CONCERNS — ambiguous signals / FAIL — critical gaps block progress]

## Completeness Overview
- Design: [X%] ([N] docs, [gaps])
- Code: [X%] ([N] files, [systems])
- Architecture: [X%] ([N] ADRs, [gaps])
- Production: [X%] ([status])
- Tests: [X%] ([coverage estimate])

## Gaps Identified
1. [Gap description + clarifying question]
2. [Gap description + clarifying question]

## Recommended Next Steps
[Priority-ordered list based on stage and role]

5. Role-Filtered Recommendations (Optional)

If user provided a role argument (e.g., /project-stage-detect programmer):

Programmer: - Focus on architecture docs, test coverage, missing ADRs - Code-to-docs gaps

Designer: - Focus on GDD completeness, missing design sections - Prototype documentation

Producer: - Focus on sprint plans, milestone tracking, roadmap - Cross-team coordination docs

General (no role): - Holistic view of all gaps - Highest-priority items across domains

6. Request Approval Before Writing

Collaborative protocol:

I've analyzed your project. Here's what I found:

[Show summary]

Gaps identified:
1. [Gap 1 + question]
2. [Gap 2 + question]

Recommended next steps:
- [Priority 1]
- [Priority 2]
- [Priority 3]

May I write the full stage analysis to production/project-stage-report.md?

Wait for user approval before creating the file.

Example Usage

# General project analysis
/project-stage-detect

# Programmer-focused analysis
/project-stage-detect programmer

# Designer-focused analysis
/project-stage-detect designer

Follow-Up Actions

After generating the report, suggest relevant next steps:

  • Concept exists but no systems index? → /map-systems to decompose into systems
  • Missing design docs? → /reverse-document design src/[system]
  • Missing architecture docs? → /architecture-decision or /reverse-document architecture
  • Prototypes need documentation? → /reverse-document concept prototypes/[name]
  • No sprint plan? → /sprint-plan
  • Approaching milestone? → /milestone-review

Collaborative Protocol

This skill follows the collaborative design principle:

  1. Question First: Ask about gaps, don't assume
  2. Present Options: "Should I create X, or is it tracked elsewhere?"
  3. User Decides: Wait for direction
  4. Show Draft: Display report summary If writing this target is not already authorized, ask: "May I write to production/project-stage-report.md?"

Never silently write files. Always show findings and ask before creating artifacts.
